cards.front: Where do rectangular rapid-flashing beacons usually sit, and how do they switch on?
cards.back: Rectangular rapid-flashing beacons switch on by push button and usually sit at crossings with no traffic signal or at mid-block crosswalks.

cards.front: What must you do while a beacon's amber lamps strobe?
cards.back: While the beacon amber lamps strobe, halt for anybody inside the crosswalk and watch for anybody about to step into it.

cards.front: What do a dark pedestrian hybrid beacon, a blinking lower yellow, and a steady lower yellow each mean?
cards.back: A pedestrian hybrid beacon sleeps dark until a walker triggers it; dark lamps mean drive through carefully, a blinking lower yellow means ease off, and a steady lower yellow means get ready to halt.

cards.front: What do the hybrid beacon's twin upper reds require when steady and when blinking?
cards.back: Once the beacon twin upper reds glow steady, stop for the crossing pedestrians; when they start blinking, stop if you have not yet done so, then roll on carefully if the crossing stands empty.

cards.front: How does the rapid-flashing beacon differ from the hybrid beacon?
cards.back: The rapid-flashing beacon answers a button with strobing amber at signal-free crossings, while the hybrid beacon answers a walker with a yellow-to-red lamp ladder.

cards.front: What separates a dark hybrid beacon from its steady twin reds?
cards.back: A dark hybrid beacon invites careful passage, while steady twin reds on the same beacon command a stop for pedestrians.

cards.front: How does strobing amber differ from blinking twin reds?
cards.back: Under strobing amber you stay stopped for crosswalk users, while under blinking twin reds you stop once and may roll on through an empty crossing.

cards.front: How should you treat a person with a harnessed service dog or a white or white-and-red cane?
cards.back: Treat a person guided by a harnessed service dog or tapping a white or white-and-red cane as likely blind, and drive with added care to keep them safe.

cards.front: Where no signs or signals govern, what does the law do about right-of-way?
cards.back: Where no signs or signals govern a meeting of road users, yield rules pick who waits; the law names who must yield but hands the right-of-way to nobody.

cards.front: Even when you hold the right-of-way, what must you still do?
cards.back: Whoever holds the right-of-way, still do all you can to keep from hitting a pedestrian or another car.

cards.front: How do yield rules relate to the crash-avoidance duty?
cards.back: Yield rules name who waits but award the right-of-way to no one, while the crash-avoidance duty binds even whoever holds it.

cards.front: How should you treat cyclists, who share the same road rights and duties?
cards.back: Bikes and cars share the same road rights and duties, yet riders crash unprotected, so drive defensively and yield to them even on occasions they should yield to you.

cards.front: Why do cyclists draw extra yielding although they carry the same road rights?
cards.back: Cyclists carry the same road rights as drivers, yet draw extra yielding because they crash unprotected.

cards.front: What ranks as the top cause of deadly traffic crashes in Iowa?
cards.back: Failing to yield the right-of-way ranks as the top cause of deadly traffic crashes in Iowa.

cards.front: When may you turn right on red?
cards.back: After a full stop you may turn right on red unless a sign bans it, yielding as you go.

cards.front: Whom does a left-turning driver wait for?
cards.back: A left-turning driver waits for oncoming cars bound straight ahead.

cards.front: How does right on red differ from a left turn in what you yield to?
cards.back: Right on red needs only a stop and a yield unless a sign bans it, while a left turn must wait out straight-bound oncoming cars.

cards.front: At an all-way stop, who goes first?
cards.back: At an all-way stop the first car to arrive leaves first after stopping fully, and when cars arrive together the one on the right moves first.

cards.front: How are all-way stop arrivals ordered?
cards.back: First to the all-way stop leaves first, while simultaneous arrivals send the rightmost car first.

cards.front: When crossing a sidewalk or using a driveway, alley, or lot, to whom do you give way?
cards.back: Crossing a sidewalk or rolling into or out of a driveway, alley, or lot, give way to people on foot.

cards.front: May a vehicle travel along a sidewalk?
cards.back: Wheels may cross a sidewalk but may never travel along it.

cards.front: Pulling onto a road from a driveway, alley, or shoulder, whom do you yield to?
cards.back: Pulling onto a road from a driveway, alley, or shoulder, yield to traffic already rolling there.

cards.front: What do you yield to when entering the road versus crossing the sidewalk?
cards.back: Entering the road you yield to rolling traffic, while crossing the sidewalk you yield to people on foot.

cards.front: Where must you stop or yield for pedestrians?
cards.back: Stop or yield for pedestrians in marked crossings and in unmarked ones alike.

cards.front: With no stop sign or signal, how do you enter an intersection?
cards.back: With no stop sign or signal, every driver slows and enters with care, all the controlled-intersection rules still bind, and extra caution rules.

cards.front: How do signed and unsigned intersections differ in their rules?
cards.back: Signed intersections spell the rules out, while unsigned ones bind the same rules plus extra caution.
cards.memory_hook: Signed spells out, unsigned adds caution

cards.front: To which vehicles must you give way?
cards.back: Give way to police cars, fire trucks, ambulances, and other emergency rigs sounding a siren or horn or flashing red or blue.

cards.front: What do you do when you spot or hear an emergency vehicle approaching from any side?
cards.back: Spotting or hearing one approach from any side, ease to the right road edge or as close right as you can get.

cards.front: What if you are inside an intersection or roundabout when an emergency rig approaches, and what about a median-split road?
cards.back: Caught inside an intersection or roundabout, drive through it before pulling aside; but on a median-split road with the rig across the divider, you need not stop at all.

cards.front: How does your response differ between open road and inside an intersection?
cards.back: Open road means ease right for the rig at once, while sitting inside an intersection means drive through it before pulling aside.

cards.front: How far must you hang back behind an emergency rig running lights and siren?
cards.back: Hang back at least five hundred feet behind a rig running lights and siren.

cards.front: How does the median-divider rule differ from the trailing rule?
cards.back: Across a median divider you need not stop for the rig at all, while trailing one you must keep five hundred feet back.

cards.front: Trailing a school bus on a two- or three-lane road, what do its flashing red or amber lamps require?
cards.back: Trailing a bus on a two- or three-lane road, its flashing red or amber lamps forbid passing and order readiness to stop.

cards.front: When the bus ahead halts with its stop arm out, how close may you stop and when may you go?
cards.back: Once that bus halts with its stop arm swung out, stop no closer than fifteen feet behind the bus and wait until the arm retracts and the bus moves again, then proceed carefully.

cards.front: Facing a school bus as its amber lamps blink, what do you do?
cards.back: Facing the bus as its amber lamps blink, slow to no more than twenty miles per hour and prepare to stop.

cards.front: When an oncoming bus stops with its arm extended on a narrow road, what do you do?
cards.back: When the oncoming bus stops with its arm extended, halt ahead of it, stay put until the arm retracts, and roll on with care.

cards.front: How do the bus lamps affect you from behind versus from ahead?
cards.back: From behind, flashing bus lamps forbid passing outright, while from ahead amber lamps only slow you to no more than twenty miles per hour

cards.front: What can breaking the school-bus stopping law cost you?
cards.back: Breaking the school-bus stopping law can cost you your license for up to one hundred eighty days.

cards.front: What two numbers attach to the halted school bus?
cards.back: The halted bus demands fifteen feet of queue space behind it, while a violation can suspend your license for up to one hundred eighty days.

cards.front: Trailing a bus on a road with four or more lanes, what do you do?
cards.back: Trailing the bus on four-plus lanes, obey the same drill: never pass on flashing red or amber, stop behind the halted bus with its arm out keeping at least fifteen feet back, and wait until the arm retracts and the bus moves.

cards.front: Meeting a stopped, armed school bus across opposite lanes on a road with four or more lanes, what may you do?
cards.back: Meeting the bus across opposite lanes on a four-or-more-lane road, you may roll past without stopping even with its lamps flashing and arm out, the single lawful pass of a stopped, armed bus.
cards.memory_hook: Wide road, oncoming bus: roll past

cards.front: Facing an armed bus, how do a narrow road and a wide road differ?
cards.back: Facing the armed bus on a narrow road you must halt ahead of it, while facing it across a wide road you may roll past.

cards.front: On a wide road, how does trailing the bus differ from facing it across the lanes?
cards.back: From behind on a wide road you stop and wait like on a narrow one, while from ahead across the lanes you are released.
